exemplar: The passage argues that the Market Revolution integrated Americans into a national capitalist economy - through transportation, communication, and new work discipline - while creating sharp new class divisions.
The Erie Canal (completed 1825) slashed freight costs between the Great Lakes and New York City, tying western farmers to eastern markets and making New York the nation's commercial capital.

The Lowell mills' young female operatives faced 12- to 14-hour days, strict boardinghouse rules, and wage cuts - conditions that sparked some of America's first industrial strikes, such as the Lowell walkouts of the 1830s.
parts: A. Briefly describe ONE claim the passage makes about the effects of the Market Revolution.
B. Briefly explain how ONE specific transportation or communication innovation contributed to the Market Revolution.
C. Briefly explain ONE way workers responded to the new industrial working conditions described in the passage.

stimulus.attribution: Original historian-style passage written for this item.
stimulus.text: Historians call the economic transformation of the early 1800s the Market Revolution: a shift from local, subsistence-oriented production to a national market economy. Canals, railroads, and the telegraph tied distant regions together; factories replaced artisan shops; and millions of Americans began working for wages under the discipline of the clock. The Market Revolution created enormous wealth and bound the nation together economically - but it also produced new inequalities between wealthy merchants and struggling workers, drew more women and immigrants into wage labor, and deepened the divide between a North embracing free-labor capitalism and a South committed to slavery.

exemplar: Columbus describes the Taino as physically impressive, generous, and technologically simple - people who had never seen steel weapons and did not understand their danger.
The Taino practiced gift-giving and communal sharing, which Columbus misread as childlike simplicity rather than a different cultural system of exchange and obligation.

Within decades the Taino population of Hispaniola collapsed - from disease, overwork in Spanish mines under the encomienda system, and violence - one of the first demographic catastrophes of the Columbian Exchange.
parts: A. Briefly describe Columbus's impression of the Native peoples he met, as expressed in the excerpt.
B. Briefly explain ONE aspect of Taino culture that shaped this first encounter.
C. Briefly explain ONE consequence of Spanish colonization for the Taino within fifty years of this encounter.

stimulus.attribution: Christopher Columbus, journal entry, October 12, 1492 (abstract by Bartolome de las Casas).
stimulus.text: They are well built, with good bodies and handsome features... They do not bear arms, and do not know them, for I showed them a sword, they took it by the edge and cut themselves out of ignorance. They would make fine servants.

exemplar: The photograph shows steerage passengers - poor immigrants crowded on an open deck - capturing the harsh, dehumanizing conditions of transatlantic migration for those who could only afford the cheapest passage.
The new immigrants came mainly from southern and eastern Europe (Italians, Poles, Russians, Jews), fleeing poverty, overpopulation, and persecution such as pogroms.
Nativists responded with restriction: the Immigration Act of 1924 established national-origins quotas that sharply limited immigration from southern and eastern Europe and excluded Asians entirely.
parts: A. Briefly describe what the photograph shows about the experience of immigrants around 1900.
B. Briefly explain ONE reason millions of 'new immigrants' came to the United States between 1880 and 1920.
C. Briefly explain ONE way nativists responded to the new immigration.

stimulus.attribution: Described from Alfred Stieglitz's photograph 'The Steerage,' 1907 (Wikimedia Commons).
stimulus.text: The photograph shows the crowded lower deck of an ocean liner: dozens of immigrant passengers in shawls and caps pressed together on an open steerage deck, gazing in different directions. A gangway divides the frame, with better-dressed passengers visible on the upper deck above - a stark image of class division at sea.
